video_title: Fed To Drop Market By 20%? | Darius Dale
gist: 42 Macro's Darius Dale argues the market-implied neutral rate has risen 50-75bp above the 3.63% effective fed funds rate, so the Fed must 'play action pass to set up the run' - hike once or twice and shrink the balance sheet to regain inflation-fighting credibility before it can ease structurally - creating roughly 15-20% summer-of-1998-style correction risk around the September/October FOMC meetings, with his quantitative KISS and Dr. Mo models already de-risking. He flags the Q3 2026 quarterly refunding announcement (dovish net financing jumping to 61% of $739bn of borrowing) as Bessent's potential bailout that could let markets trend higher instead. New Harbor's John and Mike counter that breadth is broadening (small caps, healthcare, financials, real estate) and that gold/silver/miners just printed an early bottom-fish trend change on Aug 5.

themes.theme: Fed Must Tighten Before It Can Ease

insights.claim: The market-implied neutral policy rate has risen roughly 50-75 basis points in recent months, which Darius Dale reads as the bond market demanding tighter Fed policy as the price of attracting an incremental dollar into Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Rising r* means bond yields are not just an inflation story - it argues against buying duration until the Fed acknowledges neutral has moved up.
insights.quote: it's the market's way of communicating to the Federal Reserve that you need to tighten monetary policy if you want to attract an incremental dollar of capital into the Treasury market

insights.claim: 42 Macro's implied neutral rate model puts the cutting-cycle floor at about 3.90% and the five-year-forward terminal rate at 4.15%, both above the 3.63% effective fed funds rate, implying the Fed needs one to two hikes just to reach neutral.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Concrete levels to trade against: front-end pricing of cuts is mispriced if the model is right, favoring payers/short front-end duration.
insights.quote: the Fed needs to hike by at least once a minimum or at least a minimum of once and a maximum of twice just to get back to neutral

insights.claim: Dale argues the Fed should tighten via the balance sheet rather than the policy rate, because balance-sheet tightening targets the top of the K and the financing dynamics of the AI capex cycle rather than killing the already-recessionary rate-sensitive sectors.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: If QT is the chosen tool, the pain concentrates in AI-financing credit and long-duration equities rather than in housing or small caps.
insights.quote: In our opinion we think they should do that with the balance sheet uh because it'll target you know the upper end of the K all the financing dynamics going on with the AI capex cycle

insights.claim: Dale's central Fed call is a deliberate short-term tightening designed to buy scope for durable structural easing later - 'play action pass to set up the run' - rather than a genuine hawkish regime change.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Frames any autumn hawkish surprise as a buying opportunity rather than the start of a bear market.
insights.quote: The Fed needs to play action pass to set up the run, right?

insights.claim: Dale says the Fed does not need to kill the business cycle, only slow it, describing the appropriate policy as punching the economy in the gut a couple of times to save the bond market.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Sets the expected magnitude of policy damage - a correction, not a recession - which is the key variable for whether to sell or hedge.
insights.quote: they don't have to kill the business cycle, but they should probably punch it in the gut a couple times

insights.claim: Dale believes the net output of the Fed's five internal task forces is structurally dovish, with only the communications task force (removing forward guidance, injecting rate volatility and term premium) being explicitly hawkish - a view he says is not consensus among 42 Macro's institutional clients.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: A dovish 2027 framework combined with a hawkish communications regime argues for higher rate vol (long MOVE) alongside eventual lower policy rates.
insights.quote: that's a differentiated view by the way I don't think that's consensus it certainly it certainly is not consensus among our institutional clients

insights.claim: 42 Macro models trend productivity growth rising from roughly 1-1.5% to about 3%, and Dale notes the 2-year nominal Treasury yield historically declines once trend productivity exceeds 2%, which the market reads as a signal for the Fed to cut.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: A productivity boom is the mechanism that could let the Fed ease without reigniting inflation - bullish front-end and bullish equities in 2027.
insights.quote: Our model has productivity growth going from about one one and a half% on a trend basis to about 3% on a trend basis.

insights.claim: Fed policy relative to the Taylor rule has eased across successive chairs - Volcker averaged 362bp tighter than the rule, Greenspan 65bp, Bernanke 31bp, Yellen -256bp and Powell -314bp - which Dale says is why the bond market now views the Fed as worse than Arthur Burns on credibility.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Quantifies the credibility deficit that must be paid down before easing works - supports structurally wider term premium until it is.

themes.theme: Global Bond Hot Potato and Rising r*

insights.claim: 42 Macro's core research thesis is a geopolitically driven supply and demand imbalance in the Treasury bond market, which has forced a chain of dovish policy choices including a coordinated intervention that debased the dollar to stop Japan selling Treasuries in the secondary market.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Explains why dollar debasement and gold strength are policy outputs, not accidents - structurally long gold, short dollar.
insights.quote: there was a coordinating unit intervention that required the uh bank of Japan or the federal reserve to essentially debase the dollar on behalf of the Japanese government uh in order to prevent uh the Japanese government from selling

insights.claim: Simultaneous multi-decade high yields - a near 20-year high in the 10-year Treasury, a 20-year high in the UK gilt, a 15-year high in the 10-year eurozone yield and a 30-year high in the 10-year JGB - are, per Dale, a clear signal that r* is rising globally rather than a US-specific story.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Global synchrony means duration hedges in other sovereign markets will not diversify a US bond position.
insights.quote: we got a 15-year high and the 10 year UK goat yield. We got a a near 20-year high and the 10 year Treasury yield

insights.claim: The trailing 10-year growth rate of global savings flow has collapsed to about 55% versus a long-run mean of 90%, which Dale interprets as the end of the great moderation's recycling of surplus savings into global fixed income.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: The structural bid for bonds is gone - argues for permanently wider term premium and lower bond allocations in 60/40.
insights.quote: the current growth rate is only 55% trailing 10 years versus a long run mean of 90%

insights.claim: Dale frames a global capital war in which US hyperscaler AI capex of a projected $800 billion in 2026 and $1.2 trillion in 2027 competes directly with widening US, Japanese, eurozone and Chinese deficits for a shrinking pool of global savings.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Ties AI capex financing directly to long-end yields - a reason AI credit issuance is a bond-market risk factor to monitor.
insights.quote: if you look at AI capex, US hyperscaler capex, the current projection is 800 billion for 2026, 1.2 trillion for 2027

insights.claim: Term premium remains roughly 100-110 basis points below its pre-GFC long-run mean, implying fair value on the 10-year Treasury of about 5.7% if term premium simply normalized.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: A concrete downside target for bond prices - 5.7% on the 10-year is the level to stress-test portfolios against.
insights.quote: That's fair value for 10-year treasuries.

insights.claim: Dale guarantees a 6% 30-year Treasury yield next year if the Fed fails to regain inflation-fighting credibility in the interim.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: An explicit level and timeframe - a testable bearish long-bond call to trade or fade.
insights.quote: you're going to see a 6% on a 30-year Treasury bond. I guarantee you.

insights.claim: Dale expects the modest tailwind in the monetary policy cycle to invert into a headwind over the next two to four months, particularly around the September and October FOMC meetings, which would drag the liquidity cycle into a headwind and produce summer-of-1998-style correction risk.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Gives a dated window (Sept-Oct FOMC) for de-risking or buying downside protection.
insights.quote: if those two things happen, then that's how you wind up with the summer of 1998 style correction risk

insights.claim: Dale characterizes the 1998 template as a 19% drawdown that fully retraced a 21% December-to-July rally by end-August before a 27% rally left the year up roughly 20%, implying a sharp but recoverable 15-20% equity correction.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: The historical analog says hedge the drawdown but do not exit the secular trend - the year still finishes up.
insights.quote: 19%. So the market rallied 21% I think from December through the high of July. It gave it all back and then some by the end of August and then it rallied like 27%

insights.claim: If Dale is wrong and the Fed declines to tighten cyclically, his stated alternative is not a bear market but that markets 'skate through and have a fantastic year'.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: The bear case is conditional on one policy variable - making Fed action, not fundamentals, the trigger to monitor.
insights.quote: then we're just going to skate through and have a fantastic year

insights.claim: 42 Macro's macro weather model has signaled positive for stocks, gold, Bitcoin and commodities and negative for the dollar and bonds since roughly Q2 of last year, and on net still reads structurally supportive for risk assets.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: The medium-term asset allocation stays long risk and hard assets, short duration and dollar, despite the near-term correction call.

insights.claim: Three of the top five indicators in 42 Macro's positioning model are breaching their bubble-peak mean values relative to the everything bubble, housing bubble and dotcom bubble peaks.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Positioning is at historic bubble-peak extremes, meaning any policy shock hits an unusually crowded market.
insights.quote: three of the top five indicators in our positioning model are breaching their bubble peak uh mean values

insights.claim: 42 Macro's KISS model - a simple stocks, gold and Bitcoin allocation with quantitative risk overlays - has de-risked relative to where it sat most of the year, reversing the risk-taking it began in early April.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: The systematic model is confirming the fundamental view, which historically is the higher-quality signal to act on.
insights.quote: the key takeaway is that, you know, they're moving in a way that is that is that is not not positive

insights.claim: Nominal GDP excluding government and exports is compounding at 7.8% quarter-over-quarter annualized, 7% on six months and 6.3% year-over-year, hundreds of basis points above the roughly 4% pre-COVID trend - confirmation, per Dale, that the run-it-hot strategy is working.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Above-trend nominal growth is the fundamental support for stocks-up/bonds-down, and its rollover would be the signal that the regime is ending.
insights.quote: we're compounding at 7.8%, % six-month annual high 7% year-over-year 6.3%. These numbers are hundreds of basis points above the the pre-COVID trend of four 4%

insights.claim: Dale expects growth to decelerate over the coming 12 months because the CRFB-modeled fiscal impulse from the big beautiful bill peaks at 90 basis points in 2026 and fades to 70-80 basis points in 2027, while the lagged boost from 175 basis points of rate cuts fades.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Quantifies the 2027 growth fade - a reason to expect multiple compression risk even without recession.

insights.claim: Bank credit growth accelerated from about 4% year-over-year to 7% after bank deregulation (SLR relaxation, easier liquidity stress tests, destigmatizing the discount window), but the 3-month annualized rate has slipped narrowly below trend, which Dale says will drag year-over-year credit growth and subsequently GDP.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: The 3-month annualized bank credit series is a leading indicator to watch for confirming the 2027 slowdown.

insights.claim: Dale's conclusion is that 2026 is peak paradigm C - the economy will still run nominally hot in 2027, but this is probably as good as it gets on the growth rate.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Peak growth rate with peak positioning is a classic setup for de-rating - argues for taking profits into strength rather than adding.
insights.quote: So my assumption is that we're probably peak paradigm C here in 2026.

insights.claim: Only consumer spending and AI capex are growing meaningfully in GDP, with AI capex accounting for about 30% of all growth over the last six quarters, while real residential fixed investment and non-residential structures are down roughly 5% on a six-month annualized basis.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Growth is dangerously concentrated - any AI capex pause mechanically threatens roughly a third of GDP growth.
insights.quote: basically AI capex which we know is about 30% of all growth uh over the last uh six quarters

themes.theme: Fiscal Arithmetic and the Deficit Escalator

insights.claim: Politically protected spending - Medicare, national defense, net interest and Social Security, Luke Gromen's true interest expense metric - now runs $4.7 trillion, about two-thirds of roughly $7.3-7.4 trillion of federal spending and about 15% of nominal GDP, compounding at about 9% on a trailing three-year basis.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Structural spending compounding at 9% against ~6% nominal GDP guarantees deficit widening regardless of who governs - a permanent bid for Treasury supply.
insights.quote: that's at $4.7 trillion of the budget now. So, these are politically protected categories that aren't ever going to go down.

insights.claim: The US is running nominal GDP ex-government and exports at 8% with no improvement in the budget balance as a share of GDP from fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2026, which Dale flags as evidence of zero fiscal retrenchment at the cycle peak.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: No deficit improvement at peak growth means the starting point for the next downturn is far worse than 2007 or 2019.
insights.quote: we're currently growing nominal GDP exgovernment and exports at 8% and we're having no improvement in the uh in the in the budget balance on a on a percentage of GDP basis

insights.claim: In a recession Dale estimates the deficit would widen from roughly 5-7% of GDP to 10-15% of GDP, roughly doubling the annual deficit from about $1.8 trillion to $3.6-4 trillion.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Sizes the tail scenario for Treasury supply - the case for owning gold and hard assets as recession insurance rather than bonds.
insights.quote: It'll probably double. You know, we'll go from about $1.8 8 trillion to, you know, somewhere around 3.6 to 4 trillion.

insights.claim: Roughly $2.6-2.7 trillion of federal spending flows to defense contractors and debt holders - with defense requests near $1.5 trillion likely landing around $1.15 trillion and net interest exceeding $1 trillion next fiscal year - concentrating fiscal transfers in companies like Palantir, Raytheon, Lockheed Martin and SpaceX.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Names the direct beneficiaries of the fiscal transfer - defense primes and government-adjacent tech are structurally supported regardless of the cycle.

insights.claim: Dale's Q3 2026 quarterly refunding takeaway is that the Treasury is projected to borrow $739 billion with dovish net financing jumping from roughly 20-some percent of the total to 61% in Q3 and 58% of $628 billion in Q4 - which he reads as Bessent bailing out markets while giving the Fed room to tighten.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: This is the single identified offset that could cancel the 1998 correction - the QRA composition is the thing to monitor into year-end.
insights.quote: So this in my opinion might be Scott Bessant trying to bail out the financial markets while it gives Kevin War scope to tight monetary policy.

themes.theme: K-Shaped Economy and the AI Political Backlash

insights.claim: Dale argues the fiscal and monetary regime is transferring marginal economic activity from the private sector to the public sector and its beneficiaries, financially repressing households and small businesses at the bottom of the K while supporting upper-income consumption.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Supports staying long luxury/upper-income exposure and government-linked names while avoiding low-end consumer discretionary.
insights.quote: it's coming at the expense of of consumption and investment from households and small businesses at the bottom of the K. That's who's getting financially repressed out of the economy right now.

insights.claim: Dale contends the current arrangement is sustainable in economic terms but not in political terms, and expects the political break to come after 2028 as millennials and Gen Z - now the two largest cohorts - conclude the American dream is broken.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Frames a post-2028 policy regime change risk that could invalidate the entire current investing playbook.
insights.quote: It's sustainable in economic terms but it may not be sustainable in political terms and I don't think it will be specifically once we get past 2028.

insights.claim: Dale cites polling that 68% of women think AI is advancing too fast versus only 2% of all adults who think it is too slow, and 48% of 18-29 year olds think AI will harm society, arguing AI could be the catalyst that mobilizes young non-voters.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Political backlash is an underpriced regulatory risk to AI capex and the hyperscaler trade over a multi-year horizon.
insights.quote: 68% of women think AI is advancing too fast versus only 2% of all adults who think it's going too slow

themes.theme: New Harbor: Bubble Backdrop but Broadening Breadth

insights.claim: New Harbor believes markets are in one of the biggest stock market bubbles of all time on valuation, but explicitly treats that as a non-timing signal and reports its full battery of technical indicators as strongly bullish.
insights.speaker: John, New Harbor Financial lead partner
insights.so_what: Demonstrates separating valuation from timing - the practical stance is stay invested with hedges rather than exit on valuation.
insights.quote: We certainly believe we're in one of the biggest stock market bubbles of all time, if valuations and things like that are any guide, and we think they are, even if they're not a a timing guide.

insights.claim: New Harbor's fund scores show small cap fund scores crossing above large cap scores around mid-January 2026 and holding through the recent pullback, reversing mega-cap dominance that ran from roughly 2023.
insights.speaker: John, New Harbor Financial lead partner
insights.so_what: A durable small-cap-over-mega-cap relative strength signal argues for equal-weight or small-cap tilts over cap-weighted index exposure.
insights.quote: right around mid January, the average uh small cap fund score uh exceeded the large cap fund score and it stayed uh stayed that way

insights.claim: New Harbor holds about 50% equities in its core tactical model - still underweight versus a long-term picture - plus a separate allocation to gold mining stocks.
insights.speaker: John, New Harbor Financial lead partner
insights.so_what: A concrete allocation benchmark from a bearish-leaning manager: defensive but far from flat.
insights.quote: We're about 50% in our core tactical model, 50% in equities.

insights.claim: New Harbor's trigger to lighten up is degradation in breadth - fewer stocks participating and weakening bullish percents even as indices make new highs - and they explicitly say they see the opposite right now.
insights.speaker: John, New Harbor Financial lead partner
insights.so_what: A specific, monitorable sell trigger: watch breadth deterioration at new index highs as the tell for the blowoff top.
insights.quote: what we're seeing is not a we not a weakening not a narrowing we're seeing a strengthening a broadening

insights.claim: New Harbor's sector rotation has moved out of technology's top-ranked position into laggards - exiting financials last fall into energy before the Iran-driven oil spike, then adding regional banks, healthcare and a modest diversified listed real estate position, while selling out of utilities this week.
insights.speaker: John, New Harbor Financial lead partner
insights.so_what: A live map of where relative strength is migrating - healthcare and banks showed the largest positive fund score changes.

insights.claim: New Harbor considers the Mag 7 complex to have been oversold rather than cheap, still viewing it as overvalued with an open question on whether forecast AI spend produces positive cash flow, and notes analysts project five-year earnings growth exceeding any recent five-year period.
insights.speaker: John, New Harbor Financial lead partner
insights.so_what: Treats the mega-cap bounce as a tactical oversold rally, not a fundamental re-rating - argues against chasing semis here.
insights.quote: still analysts are are predicting uh earnings growth over the next 5 years that eclipses any 5-year period in recent history. That's that's not a given. It's a it's a guess.

themes.theme: Precious Metals: Early Trend Change After Brutal Drawdown

insights.claim: On the August 5 recording day gold futures rose over $170 an ounce (roughly 4%), SLV rose 4.5% and GDX rose 7%, with gold reclaiming its 50-day moving average and challenging its 200-day after a decline that ran since the January 30 peak.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Specific levels to confirm or invalidate the reversal - the 200-day on gold and a weekly close are the immediate tests.

insights.claim: The precious metals drawdown has been severe - GDX fell from 117 to 70 (about 40%), silver more than 50% and gold nearly 40% - which Preston argues resembles 2008-09 and 1973-74 shakeouts inside larger bull markets rather than a 2011-style terminal top.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Frames the drawdown as a buyable shakeout, with the 2011 analog as the explicit bear case to disprove.
insights.quote: we think that it's more likely that this was just a big big shake in the midst of a bigger bull market

insights.claim: Mining sector bullish percents fell to roughly the 10% level, one of only three such washouts since 2020, which Preston treats as a contrarian buy extreme that previously marked GDX lows.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: A rare, quantifiable contrarian trigger with a documented track record on this specific sector.

insights.claim: Preston expects gold mining stocks could roughly double from here over the next year or two, sketching GDX moving from about 100 to 200, with a weekly break above 90 turning the decline into a confirmed basing pattern.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: An explicit price target and confirmation level for the miners trade.
insights.quote: history says we might see another double on gold stocks before they're done. So, you know, from 100 to maybe 200 on GDX in the next year or two.

insights.claim: Preston classifies the current metals setup as an early bottom-fish trend change rather than a breakout, and says if he had no position he would act now with a half-size entry, adding the balance on a weekly close higher.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Concrete entry mechanics and sizing discipline for a counter-trend metals entry - half now, half on confirmation.
insights.quote: If I if I was looking to establish a position, I didn't have one, this was when I would act right now.

insights.claim: New Harbor holds only about a 10% position in precious metals and has done rebalancing and profit-taking on the way down, arguing position sizing is what made the 50% drawdown survivable.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: A stated size band (5-10%) for high-volatility metals exposure that survives a halving without forced capitulation.
insights.quote: it's hard to be in this trade if you're oversized, but we're not oversized. We're about 10% here.
